items.articleTextTr: 'Not the answer': Labour MPs speak out against Rosebank as decision looms - Published Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments. There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland will be given the go-ahead. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that a decision would be "taken in due course" while Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stressed that affordability of energy bills was her "overriding objective". But in a sign of the division within the party, about a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns about approving it during a Westminster Hall debate in Parliament. Separately, it is understood some Labour backbenchers have organised a letter opposing Rosebank - intended for Burnham, but not yet sent - which more than 60 out of about 400 Labour MPs have indicated they support. One signatory told the BBC that approving Rosebank "would not create new jobs, would bring minimal money into the Treasury and be bad for the climate". "The government's central aim is to tackle the cost of living crisis, and drilling for more oil at Rosebank isn't the answer," the MP said. Wednesday's Westminster Hall - a type of parliamentary debate where backbench MPs raise topical issues but do not vote - was organised by Green MP Carla Denyer. Labour MP for Sheffield Central Abtisam Mohamed told the debate: "Rosebank fails on every test. "It will not benefit taxpayers who will shoulder the vast majority of the development costs, it will not strengthen our energy security because most of the oil will be sold on international markets, and it will not reduce energy bills for our constituents, who will remain exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices." Richard Burgon, a former frontbencher on the left of the party, said: "Rosebank is not compatible with our climate targets - it's dangerous to pretend otherwise." The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period. The UK government has always insisted that Rosebank is a quasi-judicial decision, formally resting with Fahnbulleh. She green-lit production in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea last month, but Rosebank hangs in the balance. Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields". Licences for both Jackdaw and Rosebank were granted by the then Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023 respectively. But the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approvals unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a fresh decision on whether to give the go-ahead. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch sought to tease at Labour divisions on the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday. Demand for fossil fuels During the debate, Labour MP Anna Gelderd said: "We live in an unprecedented era where our energy security is more vital than ever, in which jobs and wealth must be protected and economic opportunities seized - on both of these points, Rosebank fails." Labour MP Julia Buckley said she had received opposition to Rosebank from her constituents in "regularly flooded Shrewsbury" and said fossil fuels "belong in the past, not the future". She urged Fahnbulleh to "reject the oil licence in favour of renewables", adding: "Please don't add further to our climate emergency." Other Labour MPs expressed their support, including recently departed veterans minister Al Carns, who warned that Britain would continue to need fossil fuels for decades and importing more would be a mistake. "Refusing to produce it here does nothing on its own to eliminate that demand - it simply increases our reliance on imports which can carry their own environmental cost," he added. Those representing communities with ties to the oil and gas industry, including Jonathan Brash, the Labour MP for Hartlepool, stressed the benefits of approving Rosebank for British jobs. Energy minister Michael Shanks told the debate the government would take a "pragmatic approach" to a clean energy transition, stressing it was "not a turn off the taps government, but nor can we justifiably be a drill every last drop government either". "This government will not make decisions for this country which are not compatible with our climate obligations," he added. - Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm - Published25 October - Action on energy costs is my overriding aim, says Fahnbulleh - Published2 days ago - Political battle intensifies within Labour over Rosebank oil field - Published26 October Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.

items.articleText: ABD medyası yazdı: Avrupa'nın yeni kuralları Türk beyaz eşya devine yarayabilir - AB'nin Çin'den ithalata yönelik kuralları sıkılaştırma ve yerel üretimi destekleme adımları Arçelik'e avantaj sağlayabilir. Bloomberg'e göre şirket, Avrupa'daki fabrikaları sayesinde Çinli rakiplerine karşı daha güçlü konumda olmayı hedefliyor. Avrupa Birliği'nin ithalatı sıkılaştırma ve yerel üretimi destekleme adımları, Türk ihracatçılar arasında endişe yaratırken Arçelik için fırsata dönüşebilir. Bloomberg'in haberine göre şirket, Avrupa'daki mevcut fabrikaları sayesinde Çinli rakiplerine karşı avantaj elde edebileceğini düşünüyor. Avrupa'daki fabrikalar Arçelik'in elini güçlendiriyor CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Arçelik'in küresel markası Beko'nun Finans Direktörü Barış Alparslan, Türkiye'deki rekabetçi üretim yapısı ve Avrupa'daki fabrikaların şirkete önemli avantaj sağladığını belirtti. Beko'nun Avrupa'da halihazırda üretim tesislerine sahip olması, şirketin yerel üretimi desteklemeyi amaçlayan yeni AB düzenlemelerine Çinli rakiplerinden daha kolay uyum sağlamasına imkan tanıyabilir. Alparslan, Beko'nun Avrupa'daki güçlü marka bilinirliğinin de rekabette önemli rol oynadığını ifade etti. Bu konumun şirketin fiyatlarını ve satış sonrası hizmetlerini koruyarak Çinli üreticilerle rekabet etmesine yardımcı olabileceği değerlendiriliyor. Arçelik ise Avrupa'daki mevcut üretim tesisleri sayesinde yeni dönemde Çinli rakiplerinden ayrışabileceğini düşünüyor. items.title: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
items.summary: The BBC understands the discount chain, which has been edging towards administration, will be given more time to find a buyer.
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
items.summaryTr: The BBC understands the discount chain, which has been edging towards administration, will be given more time to find a buyer.
items.articleText: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue - Published Poundland and its 11,000 employees are hopeful that the retailer's impending collapse can be delayed to allow time for a last-minute rescue deal. The discount chain has been edging towards administration after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts. A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation have told the BBC that they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release of £10m in funding. A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers, Poundland's US owners, on Wednesday following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal. Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock stores and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period. The investment firm has denied the claims. But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham. About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops. However, sources close to the matter told the BBC on Tuesday that a release of £10m by its owners, while "small in the scale of things" could help at least postpone the chain's collapse while a longer term solution was explored. 'Do the right thing' Following the behind-closed-doors meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chair Liam Byrne said he was "deeply concerned" that firm's behaviour "may have jeopardised thousands of jobs on Britain's high streets". "Over the last 17 months, they have taken millions out of Poundland when the business was on a 'knife edge'," he posted on social media., external "Now Poundland appears to be on the rebound, there's concerning signs it's been strangled of access to its own funds in what should be its busiest trading period in the run up to Christmas." He claimed that Gordon Brothers refused to say it would prioritise saving jobs "over and above its own financial returns", but added the prospect of a good outcome for the business was "now higher thanks to the focus on the business of the last week". He called on Gordon Brothers "to do the right thing" and give Poundland access to its own funds and work to protect the maximum number of jobs. Views on Poundland performance differ The 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires on Thursday, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended. Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners. Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget. He added the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where there were losses of £68m. However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading". There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland stores which could mean continuing employment for workers in the event the chain is broken up and sold off in chunks. The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain. Get in touch Are you affected by issues discussed in this story? items.title: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax
items.summary: More than 6,000 Italian schools received a threat. Authorities in all three countries say there appears to be no risk to the public. It is not known if the incidents are linked.
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax
items.summaryTr: More than 6,000 Italian schools received a threat. Authorities in all three countries say there appears to be no risk to the public. It is not known if the incidents are linked.
items.articleText: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax - Published Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities. In Italy a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution but Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger". "These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook. Scotland's education secretary Mairi McAllan said there was no risk to the public and specialist cyber-crime officers were working to identify the source of the messages. In Northern Ireland education officials told schools to remain open unless otherwise advised by police. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected. "As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," McAllan said. Scottish police had earlier said that the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes. However some local authorities confirmed that some schools had been evacuated. "Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails," Police Scotland said. Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent on Wednesday to the inboxes of 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 state schools, and private schools were unaffected. The message, said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan", caused alarm in many schools. The BBC has seen the email sent to Scottish schools which appeared to have similar wording, and also referenced the name Mikhail Andropov, although as leader of a "Red Owl" project. Italy's Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the incidents involving Italian schools were probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk", adding that there appeared to be a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in across Europe targeting flights, supermarkets and even hospitals. Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption. Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings. - No risk to public from hoax school bomb threats, says government minister - Published1 hour ago - Police treating threatening email sent to more than 300 schools as 'hoax' - Published3 hours ago On Wednesday one Milan headteacher, Anna Bertato, told Italian media she had checked the email address of the sender online: "It was already classified as spam by a student at a university in Taiwan." Another Milan headteacher, Massimo Nunzio Barrella, told Adnkronos news agency that he had immediately realised the email was spam when it arrived in his inbox at 08:59 and he decided not to evacuate his school and reassured parents who phoned in. "The text seemed almost comical," said Barrella, "it was like a message from Martians: 'We have come to annihilate you.' I even had a bit of a laugh." Although many schools were initially evacuated on Wednesday, the alarm was quickly lifted, and pupils were allowed to return to class. Some parents decided to take their children home for the day, but the majority of schools in Milan did not send their pupils home. Some 280 school head teachers had already received threats in recent days, according to Italian reports. In a statement, the head of the central Umbria region Stefania Proietti said "checks conducted so far in Umbrian schools have proved negative, and law enforcement is working rapidly and carefully to verify each report". items.articleText: ABD borsasında roller değişti: Büyükler alıyor, küçükler satıyor - ABD borsalarında sert düşüşlerin ardından yatırımcıların stratejileri değişti. Bank of America verilerine göre, kurumsal yatırımcılar 6,1 milyar dolarlık alım yaparken bireysel yatırımcılar yaklaşık 2 milyar dolarlık satış gerçekleştirdi. ABD hisse senedi piyasalarında artan oynaklık, büyük yatırımcılarla bireysel yatırımcıların farklı yönlere hareket etmesine neden oldu. Bank of America'nın (BofA) yayımladığı verilere göre, son satış dalgasını fırsat olarak değerlendiren kurumsal yatırımcılar güçlü alımlara yönelirken bireysel yatırımcılar piyasadan çıkışlarını sürdürdü. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Bankanın verileri, kurumsal müşterilerin geçen hafta 6,1 milyar dolardan fazla hisse senedi satın aldığını ortaya koydu. Bu alımların yaklaşık 4 milyar dolarlık bölümünü hisse senedi borsa yatırım fonları (ETF) oluşturdu. Buna karşılık bireysel yatırımcılar üst üste dördüncü haftada da net satıcı konumunda kaldı. BofA'nın bireysel müşterileri aynı dönemde yaklaşık 2 milyar dolarlık hisse senedi sattı. Borsada alışılmış strateji tersine döndü Piyasalardaki bu ayrışma, son dönemde yatırımcı davranışlarında yaşanan değişime işaret ediyor. ABD Başkanı Donald Trump'ın 2 Nisan 2025'te açıkladığı ve "Kurtuluş Günü" olarak adlandırdığı tarife kararlarından bu yana bireysel yatırımcılar, piyasalardaki sert düşüşleri alım fırsatı olarak değerlendiriyordu. Ancak son satış dalgasında bu eğilim tersine döndü. items.titleTr: Missing 11-month-old baby found buried alive in a crate in South Carolina
items.summaryTr: Officials say the child was found close to his father's home on Tuesday, a day after he was taken, and is being cared for in hospital.
items.articleText: Missing 11-month-old baby found buried alive in a crate in South Carolina - Published An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father. Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him. The baby was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours. The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery. Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father. The search for baby Koah began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house. Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Koah. Comer was seen travelling to multiple locations without the baby and was later arrested in Lexington County without Koah. A search party of 100 police and fire department officials were then sent to search for the child, the sheriff said. He added that when they asked Comer where his son was, he "did not have much to say" about his whereabouts. Koon said that rescuers searched the woods near Comer's house and saw some "freshly disturbed dirt". As they began to dig, they heard a baby crying - something the sheriff described as "the most joyful sound you ever heard". "The race was on. Everybody was getting down there trying to get him out," Koon added. He said the crate was wrapped in a towel that probably provided enough air for Koah to survive for as long as he did, while the cold weather kept him from getting too hot. "The crate was, probably, I'm guessing about a two-foot [61cm] by two-foot dog crate. So, I think, once that crate hit the ground, he was probably up at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground," Koon explained. Of the parents relationship, the sheriff said there were "obviously some issues". Comer had previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges, court records show. Comer's mother, Patricia Comer, told NBC News that Koah's mother had full custody of him but allowed her to supervise while her son watched him. She said her son had watched the baby before unsupervised without any problems. "Honestly, I'm his mother, and I never expected this from him," Patricia Comer said.

items.title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
items.summary: Talks in Abu Dhabi centred around Europe's security framework, with US envoys due to meet Putin and Zelensky on Thursday.

items.titleTr: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
items.summaryTr: Talks in Abu Dhabi centred around Europe's security framework, with US envoys due to meet Putin and Zelensky on Thursday.
items.articleText: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough - Published Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day. Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion. However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon. Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest." "I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible. Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said. After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky. The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe. For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member. For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion. Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system. That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence. Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin. Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them. Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent. Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday. Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin. There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted. Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added. Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security. Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said. Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region. Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again. "These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this." Related topics - Published1 day ago - Published22 hours ago

items.title: Crypto Long & Short: The GENIUS Act’s guarantees don’t cover DeFi lending
